The Coding Systems: ICD, CPT, SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RadLex

Unit 1: Imaging Informatics Foundations. Lesson 4 of 65 in CIIP Academy.

A hanging protocol loads the wrong layout for knee studies. The cause is not the viewer: the same exam has three different local names across three hospitals, and the rule only recognizes one. Code sets fix this, and the exam wants you to know which one does what.

Five code sets, five jobs

Code set      Used for                            Where it appears in imaging
ICD           diagnoses and reasons for exam      order, claim
CPT           procedures and billing              order, charge, claim
SNOMED CT     clinical terms in one hierarchy     structured reports, problem lists
LOINC         observations and orderable names    orders, results, document types
RadLex        imaging terms and procedure names   reports, protocoling, indexing

RadLex Playbook

The RadLex Playbook gives standard names and codes for imaging procedures. A site maps each of its local procedure names to one Playbook entry. After that, a hanging protocol, a dose registry, a billing check, and an outside exchange can all key on the same code instead of on local spelling.

Why mapping matters

A lexicon is a list of approved terms, a coding system gives each term a code, and an ontology adds the relationships between terms, so a system can know that one finding is a kind of another.

  • Hanging protocols select layouts from the procedure code.
  • Analytics count volumes and turnaround by procedure, which only works when similar exams share a code.
  • Exchange with other organizations is clean only when both sides agree on terms.
  • Billing denials appear when the order code and the charge code disagree.

Maintenance is an operations duty

Codes change every year, and local procedure lists grow. Someone must own updates, mapping review, and retiring duplicates. That owner is named in the operations plan, not left to chance.

Exam tip: ICD says why, CPT says what was done and billed, SNOMED CT says clinical meaning, LOINC names orders and observations, RadLex names imaging terms. Mapping local names to one set is the fix for inconsistent protocols and analytics.
Remember
Each code set has one job, and mapping every local procedure name to a single standard set is what makes hanging protocols, analytics, billing, and exchange work.
Deeper explanation

The Coding Systems: ICD, CPT, SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RadLex, explained slowly

Mapping local names to one set

Three hospitals in one system name the same knee exam three ways. The hanging protocol only works for one name, the dose registry cannot compare exams, and billing finds mismatches. A mapping table solves all three.

Local name (hospital)         Standard Playbook name              Used by
KNEE 3V (north)               knee, three views                   protocol, charge
XR KNEE LT 3 VW (east)        knee, three views                   protocol, charge
Knee series (west)            knee, three views                   protocol, charge

All three map to the single standard name, and the protocol, the dose registry, and the charge rule all key on that name.

Which code does which job

Question                                   Code set
Why was this exam ordered?                 ICD
What procedure was done, and billed?       CPT
What does this finding mean clinically?    SNOMED CT
What is the order or observation called?   LOINC
What is this imaging term or procedure?    RadLex and its Playbook

Maintenance routine

  1. Quarterly, export the list of local procedure names in use.
  2. Compare it with the map and list unmapped names.
  3. Map each new name to one standard entry and record who approved it.
  4. Retire duplicates so two local names do not point at one protocol by accident.
  5. After each yearly code update, check that retired codes were replaced in orders and charges.

Worked example

Analytics shows knee exams at the north site take longer than at the east site. Before acting, check how many exams each site counts under its knee names. If the east site counts only one of its two knee names, its volume is understated and the comparison is wrong. The fault is mapping, not performance.

Why it is an operations duty

Mapping drifts every time someone adds a procedure. If nobody owns it, the drift is found only when a hanging protocol fails or a claim is denied. Naming an owner and a schedule keeps the codes alive and keeps the other systems honest.
